text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: GRANT
text: On a production line, a camera spots a hairline crack in a casting that a tired inspector would have missed at the end of a double shift. In a franchise system three hundred miles away, a forecasting model tells a store manager to prep fewer salads because rain is coming.

speaker: MAYA
text: Neither of those is a headline. Both of them are money. Welcome to the season finale of AI in the Real Economy. I'm Maya.

speaker: GRANT
text: I'm Grant. Today we cover industrial and consumer businesses, the data rights issue that can sink a deal, and then we pull the whole season together into a hundred-day plan.

speaker: MAYA
text: Manufacturing first. We mentioned the Parsec survey in episode one. Seventy two percent of manufacturers have adopted AI in some form, but only ten percent at scale. Why the gap?

speaker: GRANT
text: The survey's top barriers were implementation cost, data privacy and security, and integration with existing systems. On the floor, that usually means the data lives in a mix of machine controllers, spreadsheets and a twenty-year-old ERP, and nobody owns getting it into one place.

speaker: MAYA
text: And the use cases that work?

speaker: GRANT
text: Quality control was the top use case in that survey, and it's where I'd start too. Vision systems that inspect parts, flag defects and learn from the inspectors' decisions. The value is direct: less scrap, fewer returns, fewer warranty claims. Next is maintenance, predicting when a machine is about to fail from vibration, temperature and run-time data, so you fix it on a planned shutdown instead of an unplanned one.

speaker: MAYA
text: And off the floor?

speaker: GRANT
text: Supply chain and planning, which was the third most common use case. Demand forecasting, inventory levels, supplier risk. And then the commercial side that people forget: quoting. Many mid-sized manufacturers take days to quote a custom job because one engineer has to read the drawings. AI that drafts the quote from the drawing and past jobs can turn days into hours, and the fastest quote often wins.

speaker: MAYA
text: Any caution specific to factories?

speaker: GRANT
text: Safety. Anything that touches a physical process needs the same engineering discipline as any other change on the line. And under the EU AI Act, AI embedded in regulated products like machinery falls under the product rules, which now apply from August 2028 after this year's delay. If your portfolio company sells equipment into Europe, that's a product roadmap question, not just an IT one.

speaker: MAYA
text: Consumer businesses next. Restaurants, retail, franchise systems, consumer services.

speaker: GRANT
text: The big levers are forecasting, labor scheduling, marketing and customer service. Forecasting demand by store and by day drives food waste, inventory and staffing. Scheduling labor to that forecast is often the single biggest controllable cost. Marketing gets cheaper and more personal with AI-generated campaigns. And customer service, from order issues to booking, follows the same pattern as the phone in episode two.

speaker: MAYA
text: Franchise systems have a twist, though.

speaker: GRANT
text: They do. The franchisor doesn't control the store. So AI value depends on whether franchisees adopt the tools. The best approach I've seen is to treat AI as part of the franchise offer: build it into the system the franchisor already provides, show franchisees the results from a few early stores, and make it easier to use than not. Mandating it rarely works.

speaker: MAYA
text: And there's a brand risk.

speaker: GRANT
text: Every customer-facing AI speaks for the brand. A wrong answer about allergens or a refund policy is a brand problem, and in some cases a legal one. Keep those answers tied to approved source content, and keep a person reachable.

speaker: MAYA
text: Let's talk about the issue that a lot of operating teams miss until diligence. Data rights.

speaker: GRANT
text: Foley's piece had a sharp example. A target had trained an internal model on third-party content whose license terms barred training. The deal was repapered and the seller took a price reduction. That's the kind of thing a buyer's lawyers will find.

speaker: MAYA
text: What should an owner check now, before a buyer does?

speaker: GRANT
text: Four things. Which data each AI system was trained or tuned on, and whether you had the right to use it that way. What your vendor contracts say about your data being used to train their models. Who owns the outputs. And what your customer contracts allow you to do with their data. In services businesses, customer data is often the most valuable asset and the least documented.

speaker: MAYA
text: And insurance.

speaker: GRANT
text: As we said last episode, representations and warranties insurers are starting to exclude AI-specific risks. Clean documentation of your data rights and controls is how you keep those exclusions narrow.

speaker: MAYA
text: Let's pull it together. A fund has just closed on a non-software business. What does the first hundred days of AI look like?

speaker: GRANT
text: Days one to thirty are about finding the money. Map the five or six workflows with the most labor or the most leakage: the phone, scheduling, billing, quoting, documentation, quality. For each, put a dollar range on the opportunity using the company's own data. Missed calls times average ticket. Denied claims times average value. Scrap rate times cost. And check the data rights and vendor contracts while you're at it.

speaker: MAYA
text: Days thirty to sixty.

speaker: GRANT
text: Pick two workflows. One quick win, usually revenue capture, like after-hours calls or claim scrubbing. And one bigger bet tied to the investment thesis, like centralized dispatch in a roll-up or vision inspection in a plant. Each one gets a named business owner, a baseline, a target, and a budget. Not a pilot. A deployment with a measurement plan.

speaker: MAYA
text: And days sixty to a hundred.

speaker: GRANT
text: Ship the quick win across the whole business, not one site. Get the bigger bet live in its first location. Report results to the board in dollars: revenue captured, hours returned, cash released, defects avoided. And set up the operating rhythm: a monthly review, a short list of what's next, and controls that a buyer could audit.

speaker: MAYA
text: What role does the fund play?

speaker: GRANT
text: The fund's job is to make the decision easy and the follow-through unavoidable. Shared playbooks from other portfolio companies, a short list of vetted vendors, a few experienced operators who've done it before, and a clear expectation in the value creation plan. The company's job is to own it.

speaker: MAYA
text: So the season in a few lines.

speaker: GRANT
text: Most of the AI value in a typical portfolio lives outside software. Start where money leaks, especially the phone and billing. Put AI inside the core workflow and make the workflow owner accountable. In regulated work, AI drafts and a qualified person signs. In factories, start with quality. In franchises, make adoption the easy choice. Check your data rights before a buyer does. And measure everything in dollars.

speaker: MAYA
text: Thanks for listening to season one of AI in the Real Economy.
[OUTRO MUSIC]

speaker: GRANT
text: I'm Grant.

speaker: MAYA
text: And I'm Maya. See you next season.
